prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

The spin-lattice relaxation time, $T_{1}$, of conduction electrons is measured as a function of temperature and magnetic field in MgB$_2$. The method is based on the detection of the $z$ component of the conduction electron magnetization under electron spin resonance conditions with amplitude modulated microwave excitation. Measurement of $T_{1}$ below $T_c$ at 0.32 T allows to disentangle contributions from the two Fermi surfaces of MgB$_{2}$ as this field restores normal state on the Fermi surface part with $\pi$ symmetry only.

outputs.L1: The spin–lattice relaxation time, \(T_{1}\), of conduction electrons in MgB\(_2\) is measured as a function of temperature and magnetic field. The method is based on detecting the \(z\)-component of the conduction-electron magnetization under electron spin resonance conditions using amplitude-modulated microwave excitation. Measurements of \(T_{1}\) below \(T_c\) at 0.32 T enable the contributions from the two Fermi surfaces of MgB\(_2\) to be disentangled, because this field restores the normal state only in the portion of the Fermi surface with \(\pi\) symmetry.
outputs.L2: The temperature and magnetic-field dependence of the conduction-electron spin–lattice relaxation time, \(T_1\), is investigated in MgB\(_2\). The technique detects the \(z\)-component of the conduction-electron magnetization under electron spin resonance conditions using amplitude-modulated microwave excitation. Measuring \(T_1\) below \(T_c\) at 0.32 T separates the contributions of MgB\(_2\)’s two Fermi surfaces, because this field drives only the \(\pi\)-symmetry portion of the Fermi surface into the normal state.
outputs.L3:
The spin–lattice relaxation time, \(T_1\), of conduction electrons in MgB\(_2\) is measured as a function of both temperature and applied magnetic field. The measurement technique detects the \(z\) component of the conduction-electron magnetization under electron spin resonance conditions, using amplitude-modulated microwave excitation to probe the relaxation dynamics.

Measurements performed below the superconducting transition temperature, \(T_c\), at a magnetic field of 0.32 T make it possible to distinguish the contributions from MgB\(_2\)’s two Fermi-surface regions, associated with the \(\sigma\)- and \(\pi\)-symmetry electronic bands. At this field, the normal state is restored only in the Fermi-surface region with \(\pi\) symmetry, while the \(\sigma\)-symmetry region remains superconducting. The resulting relaxation response therefore provides a means of separating the electronic behavior of the two bands in the superconducting state.
outputs.L4:
The spin-lattice relaxation time \(T_1\) of conduction electrons in the two-band superconductor MgB\(_2\) was investigated as a function of temperature and applied magnetic field. The measurements were performed by monitoring the longitudinal, or \(z\)-component, of the electron magnetization during electron spin resonance under amplitude-modulated microwave excitation. Because the magnetization cannot follow rapid modulation when the modulation period becomes comparable to \(T_1\), the frequency dependence of the detected signal provides a direct means of determining the conduction-electron spin-lattice relaxation time.

Particular attention was paid to the superconducting state, in which MgB\(_2\) has two distinct sets of Fermi-surface sheets derived from \(\sigma\)- and \(\pi\)-symmetry electronic bands. Measurements below the superconducting transition temperature \(T_c\) were carried out in a magnetic field of 0.32 T. At this field, superconductivity is suppressed on the \(\pi\)-symmetry Fermi-surface sheets, restoring their normal-state response, while the \(\sigma\)-symmetry sheets remain superconducting. This band-selective effect makes it possible to separate the relaxation contribution of the normal \(\pi\) electrons from that of the superconducting \(\sigma\) electrons. Consequently, the temperature and field dependence of \(T_1\) provides a band-resolved probe of conduction-electron spin relaxation and of the distinct roles played by the two Fermi surfaces in MgB\(_2\).
outputs.L5:
### The MgB₂ Measurement

The measurement of MgB₂ properties is essential for understanding its behavior as a superconducting material. Magnesium diboride becomes superconducting at approximately 39 K, a comparatively high temperature for a conventional superconductor. Researchers measure its electrical resistance, magnetic susceptibility, critical current density, and magnetic-field response to evaluate sample quality and performance. Accurate measurement techniques help determine whether MgB₂ is suitable for practical applications such as superconducting wires, magnets, sensors, and energy systems.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise abstract describing how conduction-electron spin-lattice relaxation time \(T_1\) is measured in MgB\(_2\) as a function of temperature and magnetic field using amplitude-modulated ESR.
counterfactuals.output: We measure the conduction-electron spin–lattice relaxation time \(T_1\) in MgB\(_2\) using amplitude-modulated electron spin resonance (ESR). At selected temperatures and resonance fields, the microwave excitation is periodically modulated, and the in-phase and quadrature components of the ESR response are detected with a lock-in amplifier. The finite recovery time of the conduction-electron magnetization produces a frequency-dependent attenuation and phase lag. Fitting this complex response to the modulated Bloch equations, with saturation and instrumental time constants included, yields \(T_1\). Repeating the measurement over temperature and at different ESR frequencies provides the temperature- and magnetic-field dependence of \(T_1\), including changes across the superconducting transition.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize an experiment that detects the \(z\)-component of conduction-electron magnetization under electron spin resonance conditions and explains how measurements below \(T_c\) distinguish the two Fermi-surface contributions in MgB\(_2\).
counterfactuals.output:
The experiment is a longitudinally detected conduction-electron spin-resonance measurement. A static magnetic field \(H_0\parallel z\) polarizes the conduction electrons, while a transverse microwave field \(H_1\) drives ESR. The microwave power is amplitude-modulated, so resonant saturation periodically reduces the longitudinal magnetization \(M_z\). A pickup coil aligned to detect this oscillating \(z\)-component measures the response at the modulation frequency. Sweeping \(H_0\) produces the CESR spectrum; its magnitude reflects the conduction-electron spin susceptibility, while its frequency and power dependence also contain spin-relaxation information.

MgB\(_2\) is especially useful because its superconductivity resides on two distinct sets of Fermi-surface sheets:

- quasi-two-dimensional \(\sigma\) sheets with the larger superconducting gap;
- three-dimensional \(\pi\) sheets with the smaller gap.

Below \(T_c\), singlet pairing suppresses each band’s spin magnetization according to its own gap. Consequently, the measured longitudinal CESR signal cannot be described by a single-gap Yosida function. It is instead fitted as the weighted sum

\[
\chi_s(T)=\chi_\sigma\,Y[\Delta_\sigma(T),T]
          +\chi_\pi\,Y[\Delta_\pi(T),T],
\]

with the weights representing the partial Pauli susceptibilities, hence the two Fermi-surface contributions. The large-gap \(\sigma\) contribution is suppressed soon below \(T_c\), whereas the small-gap \(\pi\) contribution survives to lower temperature and is more readily restored by magnetic field. Temperature- and field-dependent measurements therefore separate the two components and provide their relative contributions to the normal-state conduction-electron magnetization.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: How can \(T_1\) measurements at 0.32 T be used to disentangle the \(\sigma\)- and \(\pi\)-band contributions in superconducting MgB\(_2\)?
counterfactuals.output:
At \(0.32\ \mathrm T\), MgB\(_2\) is in the mixed state, but the field affects its two sets of bands very differently. The small-gap, three-dimensional \(\pi\) band is strongly suppressed at fields of a few tenths of a tesla, whereas the large-gap, quasi-2D \(\sigma\) band remains superconducting. This selectivity can be exploited in \(^{11}\)B \(T_1\) measurements.

The measured relaxation rate is modeled as an additive band contribution,

\[
\frac{1}{T_1T}
 = \sum_{i=\sigma,\pi} w_i
 \int_0^\infty
 \left[N_i^2(E,H)+M_i^2(E,H)\right]
 \left(-\frac{\partial f}{\partial E}\right)dE ,
\]

where \(w_i\) contains the partial density of states and hyperfine coupling, while \(N_i\) and \(M_i\) are the quasiparticle and anomalous BCS densities of states for gap \(\Delta_i\).

At \(0.32\ \mathrm T\):

- The nearly field-independent, Korringa-like residual relaxation is mainly attributed to field-induced or nearly normal \(\pi\)-band quasiparticles.
- The strongly temperature-dependent, activated part and any remaining coherence feature mainly reflect the larger \(\sigma\)-band gap.
- Fitting \(1/T_1(T)\) with a two-gap model therefore yields the relative weights \(w_\pi,w_\sigma\), gap magnitudes, and broadening parameters.
- Comparing with higher-field normal-state data, or with different field orientations, further constrains the decomposition because the \(\sigma\)-band upper critical field is highly anisotropic while the \(\pi\) band is more isotropic.

A key caveat is that a single B nucleus couples to both bands, so the recovery curve does not normally contain separately identifiable “\(\sigma\)” and “\(\pi\)” relaxation times. The separation comes from the temperature- and field-dependent fit, with vortex-core and field-induced density-of-states effects included, rather than from assigning two exponential recovery components directly to the two bands.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a short scientific paragraph about conduction-electron spin-lattice relaxation in MgB\(_2\), mentioning temperature and field dependence, amplitude-modulated microwave excitation, and selective restoration of the normal state on the \(\pi\)-symmetry Fermi surface.
counterfactuals.output: Conduction-electron spin-lattice relaxation in MgB\(_2\) exhibits pronounced temperature and magnetic-field dependence, reflecting its two-gap superconducting electronic structure. Under amplitude-modulated microwave excitation, the associated nonequilibrium response can selectively suppress the smaller superconducting gap and restore the normal state on the \(\pi\)-symmetry Fermi-surface sheets, while the \(\sigma\)-band condensate remains comparatively robust. This band-selective response provides a sensitive probe of relaxation pathways and interband coupling in MgB\(_2\).
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a three-sentence research-summary-style description of an ESR-based method for measuring \(T_1\) in MgB\(_2\) below \(T_c\), including why a magnetic field of 0.32 T is significant.
counterfactuals.output: Field-swept X-band conduction-electron spin resonance (CESR) can be used below \(T_c\) by extracting the homogeneous ESR linewidth, correcting for vortex-induced field inhomogeneity, and converting the linewidth or saturation behavior into the quasiparticle spin–lattice relaxation time \(T_1\). Tracking this quantity versus temperature reveals how superconducting-gap opening modifies the electronic relaxation rate without requiring the much larger fields typical of NMR. The \(0.32\ \mathrm{T}\) field is the resonance field for \(g\!\approx\!2\) electrons at X-band frequencies (\(\sim9\ \mathrm{GHz}\)); it places MgB\(_2\) in the mixed state while only weakly depressing \(T_c\), enabling a comparatively low-field probe of superconducting \(T_1\).
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
